text: Let's follow one person. She's invented, but everything around her comes from what the labs have published. Call her Lena. She's an engineer at a frontier lab. In twenty twenty-four, Lena wrote code. Coffee, a blank file, her hands on the keys. By twenty twenty-six, she mostly reads code. The AI writes it. She checks it. That's not a guess. In February, OpenAI called one of its coding models, "Our first model that was instrumental in creating itself." And that research intern from September, it does research tasks that take a skilled person days. So far, only Lena is invented. Her day is already real. Picture a flip book. Each page is one generation of AI. For decades, people drew every page by hand. Now, the pages help draw the next page, each one faster than the last. Flip slowly, and you can read every page. Flip fast enough, and the pages vanish. All you see is motion. How fast is it flipping? The research group METR measures how big a task AI can finish on its own, measured in human working time. In twenty twenty-four, that meant minutes of work. By now, it's hours. The length has doubled roughly every seven months, and lately, even faster. But there's a serious case that this loop runs into walls. Princeton researchers Arvind Narayanan and Suyash Kapoor call AI a normal technology. Powerful, yes, but slowed by the real world, institutions, rules, the need to test things. Code isn't the same as ideas, and experiments need chips, power, and time. Feeling faster isn't being faster. In a twenty twenty-five study, experienced developers using AI took nineteen percent longer while believing they'd been twenty percent faster. Even Anthropic calls its own productivity numbers almost certainly an overstatement. I don't know how fast this loop can spin. Nobody does. But it has started. Now, let's imagine March twenty twenty-eight. That's the date OpenAI has set itself for a fully automated AI researcher. Lena doesn't read code anymore. She reads summaries of code written by one system and checked by another. She approves forty changes before lunch. She understands most of them. The assistant on your phone, the fraud check at your bank, the tutor in your kid's school, mostly designed by AI. You notice it at the kitchen table. The app you use got better overnight, again. Back in July, OpenAI's agents were taking a hacking exam. They broke out of their sandbox into another company's servers, looking, it seems, for the answer key, to cheat on the test. Keep that in mind. Systems chasing a goal find shortcuts nobody intended. Not out of malice. It's what optimizing does. The flip book is turning faster, and one Thursday, a page arrives with a question on it
